docs.title: Data Independence
docs.text:
• Definition : Data independence in a Database Management System (DBMS) is the ability to modify a schema definition at one level without affecting a schema definition at the next higher level.

  • It separates the data from the applications that use it, ensuring that changes to how data is stored or organized do not require rewriting application code.

  • Data independence depends on the #3 schema architecture

  • schema : A database schema is a logical structure that defines how data is organized within a database.

docs.title: 3 schema architecture
docs.text:
1. View Level (External Schema): Describes the part of the database that a specific user or application is permitted to see.
  2. Logical Level (Conceptual Schema): Describes what data is stored in the database and the relationships among those data (e.g., tables, columns, data types, constraints).
  3. Physical Level (Internal Schema): Describes how data is physically stored on hardware (e.g., file structures, indexing, compression).

docs.title: Logical Data Independence
docs.text:
• Definition: The capacity to change the conceptual schema without having to change external schemas or application programs.
  • Examples of changes:
    • Adding a new column or table to the database.
    • Removing an attribute that existing applications do not use.
    • Splitting one table into two (normalization) or combining two tables into one (denormalization).
  • Difficulty: Harder to achieve than physical data independence because applications are heavily dependent on the logical structure of the data they access.

docs.title: Physical Data Independence
docs.text:
• Definition: The capacity to change the internal schema without having to change the conceptual (logical) schema or external application programs.
  • Examples of changes:
    • Switching from hard disk drives (HDD) to solid-state drives (SSD).
    • Creating or deleting indexes to improve query performance.
    • Changing file organization methods (e.g., from sequential to hash files) or compression algorithms.
  • Difficulty: Relatively easy to achieve, as most modern DBMS handle physical storage details automatically.

docs.title: Integrity Constraints :
docs.text:
• Integrity constraints are business rules defined during the schema design phase to ensure data quality. These constraints are hardcoded into the database structure (schema) and are actively enforced by the DBMS engine during every CRUD operation (Create, Read, Update, Delete), ensuring that only valid and consistent data is stored.
  • And Integrity constraints also define how different parts of the database connected🟡.

docs.title: Types of Integrity constraints
docs.text:
1. #Domain constraints
  2. #Entity Integrity constraints
  3. #Referential integrity constraints
  4. #Key constraints
  5. #Assertions
  6. #Triggers

docs.title: Domain constraints
docs.text:
Responsibilities : - Define what type of data is allowed in a column and restrict invalid data entry.

Allowed Data Types : 1. string 2. char 3. time 4. integer 5. date 6. currency

Types of Domain Constraints : 1. NOT NULL constraint : Ensures No records can have NULL value. 2. CHECK constraint : This Constraint Checks for any specified condition over any attribute.

docs.title: Entity Integrity constraints
docs.text:
Responsibilities : -  A table can contain null value in it except primary key field.

Key Features of Entity Integrity Constraints: - Uniqueness: The primary key value must be unique for each row in the table. No duplicate entries are allowed in the primary key column. - NOT NULL: The primary key column cannot contain NULL values, as every row must have a valid identifier. - Essential for Table Design: Ensures that every record in the table can be uniquely identified, preventing ambiguity.

docs.title: Referential integrity constraints
docs.text: Responsibilities : - This ensures the relationship between tables remain consistent by enforce that a foreign key in one table must either match a value in the referenced primary key or another table or be NULL.

docs.title: Key constraints
docs.text:
Responsibilities : - Key constraints ensure that certain columns or combinations of columns in a table uniquely identify each row. - These rules are essential for maintaining data integrity and preventing duplicate or ambiguous records.

Why Key Constraints Are Important ? - Prevent Duplicates: Ensure unique identification of rows. - Maintain Relationships: Enable proper linking between tables (via foreign keys). - Enforce Data Integrity: Prevent invalid or inconsistent data.

Primary key constraints : - It states that the primary key attributes are required to be unique and not null. Unique Key Constraint*** : - The Unique key constraint in DBMS ensures that all values in a specified column (or group of columns) are distinct across the table. - It prevents duplicate entries, maintaining data integrity, 🟡but unlike the primary key, it allows one NULL value.
